sectionTitle: Induced potential, transformers and the National Grid (physics only) (HT only)

specStatements.text: If an electrical conductor moves relative to a magnetic field or if there is a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor. If the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a current is induced in the conductor. This is called the generator effect.
An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, either the movement of the conductor or the change in magnetic field.
Students should be able to recall the factors that affect the size of the induced potential difference/induced current.
Students should be able to recall the factors that affect the direction of the induced potential difference/induced current.
Students should be able to apply the principles of the generator effect in a given context.
The generator effect is used in an alternator to generate ac and in a dynamo to generate dc.
Students should be able to:
• explain how the generator effect is used in an alternator to generate ac and in a dynamo to generate dc
• draw/interpret graphs of potential difference generated in the coil against time.
Microphones use the generator effect to convert the pressure variations in sound waves into variations in current in electrical circuits.
Students should be able to explain how a moving-coil microphone works.
A basic transformer consists of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core.
Iron is used as it is easily magnetised.
Knowledge of laminations and eddy currents in the core is not required.
The ratio of the potential differences across the primary and secondary coils of a transformer Vp and Vs depends on the ratio of the number of turns on each coil, np and ns.
potential difference, Vp and Vs in volts, V
In a step-up transformer Vs > Vp
In a step-down transformer Vs < Vp
If transformers were 100% efficient, the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input.
V_s × I_s = V_p × I_p
Where Vs × Is is the power output (secondary coil) and Vp × Ip is the power input (primary coil).
power input and output, in watts, W
Students should be able to:
• explain how the effect of an alternating current in one coil in inducing a current in another is used in transformers
• explain how the ratio of the potential differences across the two coils depends on the ratio of the number of turns on each
• calculate the current drawn from the input supply to provide a particular power output

• apply the equation linking the p.d.s and number of turns in the two coils of a transformer to the currents and the power transfer involved, and relate these to the advantages of power transmission at high potential differences.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of laminations and eddy currents in the core is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The transformer core is treated here exactly as the specification treats it: a piece of iron, used because iron is easily magnetised, whose job is to carry the changing magnetic field from the primary coil to the secondary coil. Nothing in the concepts, misconceptions or questions mentions laminations, eddy currents, hysteresis, or any account of transformer inefficiency based on them. Where efficiency appears it is only in the form the specification uses — the conditional statement that if a transformer were 100% efficient the power output would equal the power input — and no cause of real-world losses in the core is named or asked about. Questions about why iron is chosen are answered solely by 'iron is easily magnetised', and questions about why alternating current is needed are answered by the changing magnetic field, never by eddy-current arguments.

concepts.definition: If an electrical conductor moves relative to a magnetic field, or if there is a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor. This is called the generator effect. What matters is the change: a conductor sitting still in an unchanging magnetic field has no potential difference induced across it.
The potential difference produced across the ends of a conductor by the generator effect. It appears across the ends of the conductor whether or not the conductor is part of a complete circuit.

If the conductor across which a potential difference is induced is part of a complete circuit, a current is induced in the conductor. A complete circuit is needed for the current, but not for the potential difference.

An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change — either the movement of the conductor or the change in magnetic field. This is why a magnet pushed towards a coil is pushed back by the coil, and why a generator becomes harder to turn once its output circuit is completed.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the size of the induced potential difference
concepts.definition: The induced potential difference (and so the induced current) is larger if the conductor or magnet moves faster, if a stronger magnet or magnetic field is used, and if the coil has more turns. All three increase how quickly the magnetic field through the coil changes.

concepts.term: Factors affecting the direction of the induced potential difference
concepts.definition: The direction of the induced potential difference and induced current is reversed by reversing the direction of motion of the conductor or magnet, and by reversing the direction (polarity) of the magnetic field. Reversing both together leaves the direction unchanged.

A generator that uses the generator effect to produce alternating current (ac). A coil is rotated in a magnetic field, and the ends of the coil are connected through slip rings and brushes to the external circuit. Because each side of the coil moves first one way then the other through the field, the induced potential difference reverses every half turn.

The pair of rings in an alternator that keep each end of the rotating coil permanently connected to the same output terminal. Because the connections are never swapped over, the reversal of the induced potential difference in the coil is passed straight to the external circuit, giving ac.

A generator that uses the generator effect to produce direct current (dc). It works in the same way as an alternator, but the coil is connected to the external circuit through a split-ring commutator instead of slip rings, so the output potential difference never reverses.

The split ring in a dynamo that swaps the connections between the coil and the external circuit every half turn. The induced potential difference in the coil still reverses each half turn, but because the connections reverse at the same moment the output potential difference always acts in the same direction.

concepts.term: Potential difference–time graph for an alternator
concepts.definition: A wave that alternates above and below the zero line: the potential difference rises to a peak in one direction, falls back through zero, rises to a peak in the opposite direction, and returns to zero. One complete rotation of the coil produces one complete cycle.

concepts.term: Potential difference–time graph for a dynamo
concepts.definition: A series of repeated humps that all lie on the same side of the zero line. The output still rises and falls to zero twice per rotation, but it never becomes negative, because the split-ring commutator reverses the connections each half turn.

A device that uses the generator effect to convert the pressure variations in a sound wave into variations in current in an electrical circuit. The pressure variations make a diaphragm vibrate; a coil attached to the diaphragm moves in the field of a permanent magnet; this relative movement induces a potential difference and so a current in the coil. The current varies with the same frequency as the sound wave, and a louder sound moves the diaphragm and coil further and faster, giving a larger current.

A basic transformer consists of a primary coil and a secondary coil wound on an iron core. The two coils are not electrically connected to each other; they are linked only by the magnetic field carried through the iron core.

Iron is used for the core as it is easily magnetised. The changing current in the primary coil can therefore set up a changing magnetic field in the core readily, and that changing field passes through the secondary coil.

The ratio of the potential differences across the primary and secondary coils, Vp and Vs, depends on the ratio of the number of turns on each coil, np and ns: Vp/Vs = np/ns, with potential difference Vp and Vs in volts, V. In the AQA specification this equation is given on the Physics equation sheet, so it does not have to be recalled — but it does have to be selected, rearranged and used correctly.

A transformer in which Vs > Vp, so the potential difference across the secondary coil is greater than the potential difference across the primary coil. This requires more turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil.

A transformer in which Vs < Vp, so the potential difference across the secondary coil is smaller than the potential difference across the primary coil. This requires fewer turns on the secondary coil than on the primary coil.

If transformers were 100% efficient, the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input: Vs × Is = Vp × Ip, where Vs × Is is the power output (secondary coil) and Vp × Ip is the power input (primary coil), with power input and output in watts, W. Like the turns-ratio equation, this is given on the AQA Physics equation sheet. Because the product of potential difference and current is fixed, raising the potential difference must lower the current, and lowering the potential difference must raise the current.

concepts.term: Why a transformer needs an alternating current
concepts.definition: An alternating current in the primary coil produces a continuously changing magnetic field in the iron core. That changing field passes through the secondary coil, and a changing magnetic field around a conductor induces a potential difference — so an alternating potential difference is induced across the secondary coil. A steady direct current would give a steady magnetic field, which does not change and so induces nothing.

For a given power transferred, Vs × Is = Vp × Ip means that a higher potential difference goes with a smaller current. Since the energy wasted heating the transmission cables depends on the current in them, transmitting at a high potential difference and a low current wastes less energy and makes transmission more efficient. Step-up transformers raise the potential difference for transmission and step-down transformers lower it again for use.

misconceptions.question: A coil of wire is connected only to a sensitive ammeter, with no cell in the circuit. Can a current flow in it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Moving a magnet near the coil induces a potential difference across the coil, and because the circuit is complete a current is induced.
misconceptions.misconception: You can't get a current without a battery — something has to push the charge round, and a magnet isn't a power supply.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every circuit a student has built before this topic contains a cell, and 'the cell drives the current' is the rule they have been taught for two years. Nothing in that rule prepares them for a source of potential difference that is a piece of moving metal.
misconceptions.correction: The generator effect is itself a source of potential difference. Relative movement between a conductor and a magnetic field, or a change in the magnetic field around a conductor, induces a potential difference across the conductor's ends — no cell required. That is exactly how every power station generates its electricity.

misconceptions.question: Does it matter whether you move the magnet or move the coil?
misconceptions.correct: No. What is required is relative movement between the conductor and the magnetic field; either one may be the thing that moves.
misconceptions.misconception: The magnet is what does the work, so the magnet has to be the thing that moves. If the magnet is held still, nothing can happen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Demonstrations almost always show a magnet being pushed into a stationary coil, and the magnet is the 'active' object in the student's mental picture. Relative motion is a harder idea than 'the magnet moves'.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says the conductor moves relative to the magnetic field. Moving the coil over a stationary magnet changes the magnetic field through the coil in exactly the same way, and induces exactly the same potential difference.

misconceptions.question: A bar magnet is pushed into a coil and then held still inside it. Is there a current while it is held still?
misconceptions.correct: No. There is a current only while the magnet is moving. Once it is stationary the field through the coil is not changing, so nothing is induced.
misconceptions.misconception: The magnet inside the coil is what makes the current, so as long as the magnet stays inside, current keeps flowing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read the magnet as the source, in the same way a cell is a source: put it in place and it supplies current continuously. The idea that it is the *change* that matters, not the presence, is genuinely counter-intuitive.
misconceptions.correction: The generator effect needs relative movement or a changing magnetic field. A magnet resting inside a coil produces a steady field through it, nothing is changing, and the meter reads zero. Only the moving-in and the moving-out give a reading.

misconceptions.question: A single wire, not connected to anything, is moved through a magnetic field. Is anything induced?
misconceptions.correct: Yes — a potential difference is induced across the ends of the wire. There is no current, because the circuit is not complete.
misconceptions.misconception: If the circuit isn't complete then nothing at all happens; no circuit, no electricity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Current needs a complete circuit' is a rule students apply well, and they over-extend it to potential difference, which they have not clearly separated from current.
misconceptions.correction: The specification separates the two: a potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor, and *if* the conductor is part of a complete circuit, a current is induced. Potential difference first, current only when there is a path.

misconceptions.question: A magnet is pushed into a coil. Does the magnetic field made by the induced current help or hinder the magnet?
misconceptions.correct: It opposes the change — the coil's induced magnetic field pushes back against the magnet being pushed in.
misconceptions.misconception: The coil becomes an electromagnet, and magnets attract, so the coil pulls the magnet in and helps it along.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know an induced current makes a magnetic field, and their default expectation of any two magnets is attraction. Nothing in their experience suggests the coil would fight the motion that created it.
misconceptions.correction: An induced current always generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change, whether that change is the movement of the conductor or a change in the magnetic field. If it helped instead, you would get energy for nothing — the opposition is why work has to be done to turn a generator.

misconceptions.question: Does pushing a magnet further into a coil give a bigger reading than pushing it in faster?
misconceptions.correct: No. Speed is what matters. Moving the magnet faster gives a larger induced potential difference; moving it a longer way at the same speed does not.
misconceptions.misconception: The more you move the magnet, the more current you get — a bigger movement means a bigger reading.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'More movement gives more effect' is a reasonable general expectation, and students conflate the *size* of the movement with the *rate* of the movement, which are separate quantities they rarely have to distinguish.
misconceptions.correction: The size of the induced potential difference depends on how quickly the field through the coil changes. Faster movement, a stronger magnet and more turns on the coil all increase it. Distance moved at the same speed only makes the reading last longer, not grow larger.

misconceptions.question: A magnet is pushed into a coil and the meter kicks to the right. Which way does it kick as the magnet is pulled out?
misconceptions.correct: To the left. Reversing the direction of the movement reverses the direction of the induced potential difference and current.
misconceptions.misconception: The magnet drives the current one particular way, so the needle always goes the same way whatever you do with the magnet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: By analogy with a cell, which has a fixed positive terminal, students expect a magnet to have a fixed 'current direction' built into it. The reversal on withdrawal often gets dismissed as the meter settling back.
misconceptions.correction: The direction of the induced potential difference is reversed by reversing the direction of motion, and also by reversing the polarity of the magnetic field — for example by pushing in the south pole instead of the north pole. Pushing in and pulling out give opposite deflections.

misconceptions.question: What is the difference between an alternator and a dynamo?
misconceptions.correct: The alternator uses slip rings and generates ac; the dynamo uses a split-ring commutator and generates dc.
misconceptions.misconception: A dynamo must spin the other way round, or use different magnets — that's why the current comes out the other kind.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for the difference in the parts they find most vivid, the magnets and the spinning, rather than in the small ring assembly at the axle, which diagrams often draw faintly and which is easy to skip past.
misconceptions.correction: Everything else can be identical. The single difference that matters is how the coil is connected to the external circuit: slip rings keep each end of the coil on the same terminal, giving ac, while a split-ring commutator swaps the connections every half turn, giving dc.

misconceptions.question: In a dynamo, is the potential difference induced in the coil itself direct?
misconceptions.correct: No. The induced potential difference in the rotating coil still reverses every half turn; it is the split-ring commutator that makes the output direct.
misconceptions.misconception: A dynamo makes dc, so the coil inside must be producing a one-way potential difference all along.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason backwards from the output to the source, assuming a dc output must come from a dc origin, because they have never met a device that converts one to the other mechanically.
misconceptions.correction: Any coil rotating in a magnetic field has an alternating potential difference induced in it, because each side of the coil moves one way through the field and then the other. The commutator reverses the external connections at the same instant, so the output stays one way round.

misconceptions.question: An alternator's coil is spun faster. Do the peaks on the potential difference–time graph change height?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Spinning faster gives taller peaks as well as peaks that come more often.
misconceptions.misconception: Spinning it faster just squashes the same wave up — the peaks come closer together but they stay the same height.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The change in spacing is visually obvious and easy to reason about (one cycle per turn), so students stop there. Linking rotation speed to the *size* of the induced potential difference requires bringing in a separate fact from 4.7.3.1.
misconceptions.correction: Speed of movement is one of the factors that affects the size of the induced potential difference, so a faster spin raises the peak potential difference. It also fits more cycles into the same time. Both changes happen together.

misconceptions.question: What does the potential difference–time graph of a dynamo look like?
misconceptions.correct: A series of repeated humps that stay on the same side of the zero line, rising and falling but never going negative.
misconceptions.misconception: Dc means a steady value, so a dynamo's graph must be a flat horizontal line, like a battery's.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Dc' has been taught as the kind of supply a cell gives, and the graph students have seen for a cell is a horizontal line. Dc is then remembered as 'constant' rather than as 'always in the same direction'.
misconceptions.correction: Direct means one direction, not constant size. The dynamo's output rises and falls twice per rotation as the coil turns, but the commutator stops it ever reversing, so the trace is a row of humps all above the zero line.

misconceptions.question: In a moving-coil microphone, what makes the coil move?
misconceptions.correct: A diaphragm, which is made to vibrate by the pressure variations in the sound wave, and which the coil is attached to.
misconceptions.misconception: A current is sent through the coil and that makes it move — the microphone works like a small loudspeaker.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Microphones and loudspeakers contain the same parts and are usually taught in the same lesson, so students merge them. The motor effect is met first, and its 'current makes things move' logic is applied here too.
misconceptions.correction: A microphone runs the process the other way. Sound moves the diaphragm and coil, the coil moves relative to the permanent magnet's field, and that relative movement induces a potential difference and a current. It is the generator effect, not the motor effect.

misconceptions.question: A note is sung more loudly into a microphone. What changes in the current produced?
misconceptions.correct: The current is larger. Its frequency is unchanged, because the pitch of the note has not changed.
misconceptions.misconception: Louder means more energy, so the current must be going up and down more times each second.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Amplitude and frequency are persistently confused across the whole of waves, and 'more' is mapped onto whichever wave property the student thinks of first. The two axes of a graph are also easy to swap.
misconceptions.correction: Loudness comes from the size of the pressure variations, so a louder note moves the diaphragm and coil further and faster and induces a larger current. Frequency of the current follows the frequency of the sound wave, which is set by the pitch of the note.

misconceptions.question: Are the primary and secondary coils of a transformer connected to each other?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are separate circuits, linked only by the changing magnetic field carried through the iron core.
misconceptions.misconception: The iron core carries the electricity across from the primary coil to the secondary coil, because iron is a metal and metals conduct.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see a metal path joining the two coils and apply the only rule they have for metals in circuits: they conduct, so current flows through them. The idea of a magnetic link doing the job instead is new here.
misconceptions.correction: What crosses the core is a changing magnetic field, not a current. The changing current in the primary coil magnetises the core, the core's changing field passes through the secondary coil, and that changing field induces a potential difference across the secondary coil.

misconceptions.question: Why is the core of a transformer made of iron?
misconceptions.correct: Iron is used as it is easily magnetised.
misconceptions.misconception: Iron is used because it is a good conductor of electricity, so it carries the electricity between the coils efficiently.
misconceptions.whyItArises: It follows directly from the belief that the core conducts current across, and 'metals are good conductors' is a far more familiar fact to reach for than 'iron is easily magnetised'.
misconceptions.correction: The core's job is magnetic, not electrical. Iron is chosen because it is easily magnetised, so the changing current in the primary coil produces a strong changing magnetic field in the core, which then passes through the secondary coil.

misconceptions.question: Will a transformer work if it is connected to a battery instead of the mains?
misconceptions.correct: No. A steady direct current gives a steady magnetic field in the core, which is not changing, so nothing is induced across the secondary coil.
misconceptions.misconception: Electricity is electricity — a transformer will step a battery's voltage up or down just as well as the mains.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat the transformer as a device that acts on 'voltage' as a quantity, rather than as a device whose whole operation depends on the field changing. The ac requirement is easy to leave out of the explanation.
misconceptions.correction: The transformer depends on an alternating current in the primary coil producing a continuously changing magnetic field in the core. Only a changing magnetic field around the secondary coil induces a potential difference across it, so a steady dc supply produces no output.

misconceptions.question: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 400 on the secondary. Is the secondary potential difference larger or smaller?
misconceptions.correct: Larger — four times the primary potential difference, because the secondary has four times as many turns.
misconceptions.misconception: More turns means more wire for the electricity to fight through, so the secondary voltage comes out smaller.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students substitute into Vp/Vs = np/ns without tracking which coil is which, and the resistance-of-longer-wire idea from electricity gives a plausible-sounding reason for the upside-down answer.
misconceptions.correction: The potential differences are in the same ratio as the turns: Vp/Vs = np/ns. The coil with more turns has the larger potential difference across it. Always label which coil is primary and which is secondary before substituting.

misconceptions.question: Does a step-up transformer increase the electrical power?
misconceptions.correct: No. If a transformer were 100% efficient the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input; a step-up transformer raises the potential difference only.
misconceptions.misconception: A step-up transformer boosts the electricity, so you get more power out than you put in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Step-up' sounds like an increase in everything, and students who have not separated potential difference from power read a rise in volts as a rise in energy delivered per second.
misconceptions.correction: Vs × Is = Vp × Ip. The power output equals the power input for a 100% efficient transformer, so raising the potential difference must be paid for by lowering the current. A transformer redistributes power between potential difference and current; it never creates it.

misconceptions.question: In a step-up transformer, what happens to the current in the secondary coil?
misconceptions.correct: It is smaller than the primary current, because the power output cannot exceed the power input.
misconceptions.misconception: A step-up transformer steps everything up, so the current in the secondary is bigger too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Potential difference and current are treated as one undifferentiated idea called 'the electricity', so anything that increases one is assumed to increase the other. Ohm's law reasoning (more volts, more current) reinforces it.
misconceptions.correction: Use Vs × Is = Vp × Ip. If Vs is greater than Vp then Is must be less than Ip for the products to be equal. Stepping the potential difference up always steps the current down, and this is exactly what makes high-potential-difference transmission useful.

misconceptions.question: Why is power sent across the National Grid at hundreds of thousands of volts?
misconceptions.correct: Because for the same power a higher potential difference means a smaller current, and a smaller current wastes less energy heating the cables.
misconceptions.misconception: A higher voltage gives the electricity a bigger push, so it can travel further along the cables without running out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Voltage pushes current' is a serviceable model in simple circuits, and students extend it to distance: more push, further travel. The real argument — that the loss depends on the current — is one step removed from anything they can see.
misconceptions.correction: Charge is not 'used up' along the line. The energy wasted heats the cables and depends on the current in them, so the aim is a small current. Since Vs × Is = Vp × Ip, transmitting a given power at a high potential difference means a low current and less wasted energy.

misconceptions.question: On a potential difference–time graph, what happens to the spacing of the peaks if the coil spins faster?
misconceptions.correct: The peaks come closer together, because more complete rotations, and so more complete cycles, fit into the same time.
misconceptions.misconception: Spinning faster stretches the wave out, so the peaks end up further apart.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'faster' with 'bigger' on the graph as a whole, and without firmly linking one rotation to one cycle they have no anchor for what the horizontal axis is measuring.
misconceptions.correction: One complete rotation of the coil produces one complete cycle of the graph. More rotations per second means more cycles per second, so the peaks are closer together — and, since faster movement induces a larger potential difference, they are also taller.

misconceptions.question: A transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 400 on the secondary. What is the secondary potential difference?
misconceptions.correct: It cannot be found from the turns alone — you need the primary potential difference, and then multiply it by the turns ratio of 4.
misconceptions.misconception: The turns ratio is 4, so the answer is 4 V — the ratio is the voltage.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Under pressure students compute the easy quantity, the ratio, and then hand it in with a unit attached. The ratio is a pure number and has no units at all, but that is rarely said out loud.
misconceptions.correction: Vp/Vs = np/ns relates two ratios. The turns ratio tells you the factor by which the potential difference changes, not the potential difference itself. Multiply the primary potential difference by that factor to get the secondary potential difference in volts.

misconceptions.question: Is the current in the secondary coil of a transformer the same as the current in the primary coil?
misconceptions.correct: Usually not. The two coils are separate circuits, and the currents are related by Vs × Is = Vp × Ip.
misconceptions.misconception: It's all one device, so the current going in must be the current coming out — like a series circuit, where the current is the same everywhere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Current is the same all the way round a series circuit' is a rule students have used constantly and correctly, and a transformer looks like one object rather than two circuits that are not joined.
misconceptions.correction: The primary and secondary coils form two separate circuits linked only by a magnetic field, so the series rule does not apply across them. For a 100% efficient transformer, Vs × Is = Vp × Ip, so a smaller secondary potential difference goes with a larger secondary current.

misconceptions.question: The induced current in a coil makes a magnetic field that opposes the change. Does that field cancel the magnet's field completely?
misconceptions.correct: No. It opposes the change, making the magnet harder to push in, but it does not wipe out the magnet's field.
misconceptions.misconception: 'Opposes' means it exactly cancels the other field out, so there is no magnetic field left inside the coil at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Opposes' is read as the strong word 'cancels', helped by experience of balanced forces cancelling to zero. Students do not notice that a complete cancellation would remove the very change that induces the current.
misconceptions.correction: The induced field acts against the original change — the movement of the conductor, or the change in the magnetic field — which is felt as a resisting push or a generator that is harder to turn. If it cancelled the change entirely there would be no change left to induce anything.

mcqs.stem: A student pushes a bar magnet into a coil of wire that is connected to a sensitive ammeter. There is no cell in the circuit. What does the meter show while the magnet is moving in?

options.text: A current, because the magnetic field through the coil is changing
options.rationale: A change in the magnetic field around a conductor induces a potential difference, and since the circuit is complete a current is induced.

options.text: No current, because there is no cell or battery in the circuit
options.rationale: The student's rule is that a current needs a driving cell, and no cell is visible here.

options.text: No current, because a current appears only once the magnet is still
options.rationale: Treats the magnet's presence inside the coil, rather than its motion, as the source of the current.

options.text: A current only in the half of the coil the magnet has entered
options.rationale: Imagines the effect as local to the part of the coil the magnet is next to, rather than a potential difference across the whole coil.

mcqs.stem: A bar magnet is clamped so that it cannot move. A coil connected to a voltmeter is then moved down over the magnet. What happens?

options.text: No pd is induced, because the magnet itself is not moving
options.rationale: The student treats the magnet as the active partner that must move for anything to happen.

options.text: A pd is induced, since the conductor moves relative to the field
options.rationale: The specification requires only that the conductor moves relative to the magnetic field; which of the two actually moves is irrelevant.

options.text: No pd is induced, because the circuit contains no cell
options.rationale: Applies the familiar rule that a source of potential difference must be a cell.

options.text: A pd is induced across the magnet, not across the coil
options.rationale: Confuses where the potential difference appears, placing it on the object the student sees as the source.

mcqs.stem: A single straight wire, with both ends left unconnected, is moved downwards between the poles of a strong magnet. What is induced?

options.text: Nothing at all, because the circuit is not complete
options.rationale: Over-extends the correct rule about current to potential difference as well.

options.text: A current in the wire, which flows back and forth inside it
options.rationale: Invents a way for current to exist without a circuit rather than accepting a potential difference with no current.

options.text: A pd across the ends of the wire, but no current flows
options.rationale: A potential difference is induced across the ends of the conductor; a current is induced only if the conductor is part of a complete circuit.

options.text: Nothing, because the wire has no cell to drive a current
options.rationale: Falls back on the rule that electrical effects require a cell.

mcqs.stem: A magnet is pushed north-pole-first into a coil that is part of a complete circuit. The induced current produces its own magnetic field. What does that field do?

options.text: It helps the magnet's motion, so the coil pulls it inwards
options.rationale: The student expects magnets to attract, and sees no reason the coil would resist.

options.text: It cancels the magnet's field, leaving no field in the coil
options.rationale: Reads 'opposes' as 'exactly cancels', which would leave no change at all and so no induced current.

options.text: It acts at right angles to the magnet's own magnetic field
options.rationale: Borrows the right-angle relationship met in the motor effect and applies it here.

options.text: It opposes the magnet's motion, so the coil pushes it back
options.rationale: An induced current generates a magnetic field that opposes the original change — here, the movement of the magnet towards the coil.

mcqs.stem: A hand-cranked generator turns easily when nothing is connected to it. It becomes noticeably harder to turn as soon as a lamp is connected across its output. Why?

options.text: The induced current sets up a field that opposes the rotation
options.rationale: Completing the circuit allows an induced current, whose magnetic field opposes the original change — the movement of the coil.

options.text: The induced current sets up a field that speeds the coil up
options.rationale: If the induced field helped the motion the generator would get easier to turn, which is what a student expecting attraction predicts.

options.text: The magnets pull harder on the coil once the circuit is closed
options.rationale: Blames the permanent magnets, which are unchanged, rather than the field of the induced current.

options.text: The lamp's resistance pushes the current back the wrong way
options.rationale: Reasons about the lamp as though it were opposing a supply, in the way a cell-driven circuit would be analysed.

mcqs.stem: A magnet is moved into a coil connected to a voltmeter. Which change would increase the size of the induced potential difference?

options.text: Moving the same magnet into the coil over a longer path
options.rationale: Confuses how far the magnet moves with how fast it moves; a longer path at the same speed only lasts longer.

options.text: Moving the same magnet into the coil more quickly
options.rationale: Speed of movement is one of the factors affecting the size of the induced potential difference: a faster change gives a larger reading.

options.text: Holding the magnet still closer to the centre of the coil
options.rationale: Treats being deep inside the coil, rather than moving, as what produces the reading.

options.text: Using a coil of thicker wire with the same number of turns
options.rationale: Thicker wire lowers the coil's resistance but does not change the rate at which the field through it changes.

mcqs.stem: The coil of a generator is spun faster than before, with the same magnets. What happens to the induced potential difference?

options.text: It stays the same, but the current lasts for a longer time
options.rationale: Keeps the size fixed and puts the change into duration instead, the classic rate-versus-amount confusion.

options.text: It decreases, because the coil spends less time in the field
options.rationale: Assumes the coil needs time in the field to build up a reading, as though charge accumulated.

options.text: It increases, because the field through the coil changes faster
options.rationale: Faster relative movement means a faster change in the magnetic field through the coil, and so a larger induced potential difference.

options.text: It stays the same, because the magnets have not been changed
options.rationale: Attributes the size of the output solely to the magnets, so a change of speed is thought to alter only timing.

mcqs.stem: A magnet is pushed into a coil and the meter needle deflects to the right. The same magnet is then pulled straight back out again. What does the needle do?

options.text: It deflects to the right again, by the same amount
options.rationale: The student believes the magnet has a fixed current direction built into it, like a cell's terminals.

options.text: It deflects to the right, but by a smaller amount
options.rationale: Keeps the direction fixed and varies the size instead, as if the effect faded with distance.

options.text: It shows no deflection until the magnet is fully out
options.rationale: Treats withdrawal as the removal of a source rather than as a change in the field.

options.text: It deflects to the left, since the motion has reversed
options.rationale: Reversing the direction of movement reverses the direction of the induced potential difference and current.

mcqs.stem: A magnet is pushed north-pole-first into a coil, inducing a current in one direction. Which change would reverse the direction of that induced current?

options.text: Pushing the magnet in south pole first instead of north first
options.rationale: Reversing the polarity of the magnetic field reverses the direction of the induced potential difference and current.

options.text: Pushing the magnet in faster than it was pushed in before
options.rationale: Chosen by students who do not connect direction to the field's polarity and pick the only change they can see.

options.text: Pushing the magnet further into the coil than it went before
options.rationale: Confuses the amount of movement with the properties that set the direction.

options.text: Using a coil with twice as many turns of the same wire
options.rationale: More turns increases the size of the induced potential difference but does not reverse it.

mcqs.stem: A bicycle lamp is powered by a small generator whose wheel is pressed against the moving tyre. The lamp dims as the cyclist slows down. Why?

options.text: The coil turns through a smaller angle on each rotation
options.rationale: Substitutes an amount of movement for a rate of movement; a rotation is a rotation whatever the speed.

options.text: The coil turns more slowly, so a smaller pd is induced
options.rationale: Applying the generator effect: slower relative movement means a slower change of field and a smaller induced potential difference.

options.text: The pd is unchanged, but it now reaches the lamp less often
options.rationale: Holds the size of the output fixed and puts the whole effect of speed into timing.

options.text: The magnet inside becomes weaker as the generator cools
options.rationale: Invents a change in the permanent magnet rather than in the rate of movement.

mcqs.stem: A seismometer has a heavy magnet hanging on a long spring inside a coil that is fixed to the ground. During a tremor the ground and the coil shake while the heavy magnet stays almost still. What happens in the coil's circuit?

options.text: No pd is induced, because the magnet itself stays still
options.rationale: The student requires the magnet to be the moving part before anything can be induced.

options.text: No pd is induced, as the spring supplies no electrical energy
options.rationale: Looks for a conventional energy source in the circuit and, finding none, concludes nothing happens.

options.text: A pd is induced, as coil and field move relative to each other
options.rationale: The generator effect requires relative movement between the conductor and the magnetic field, which is exactly what the shaking produces.

options.text: A pd is induced only at the moment the tremor stops
options.rationale: Associates the reading with the coil coming to rest in a new position rather than with the movement itself.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about alternators and dynamos is correct?

options.text: An alternator generates dc and a dynamo generates ac
options.rationale: The two names are simply swapped over — an easy slip for a student who has learned the pairing by rote.

options.text: Both generate ac, but the dynamo spins the other way
options.rationale: Locates the difference in the rotation rather than in the ring connections.

options.text: Both generate dc, but the alternator's coil spins faster
options.rationale: Assumes any rotating coil gives dc, and looks for the difference in the speed of spinning.

options.text: An alternator generates ac and a dynamo generates dc
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states: the generator effect is used in an alternator to generate ac and in a dynamo to generate dc.

mcqs.stem: What is the job of the pair of slip rings in an alternator?

options.text: To keep each end of the coil joined to the same output terminal
options.rationale: Because the connections are never swapped, the reversal of the induced potential difference in the coil appears in the output, giving ac.

options.text: To swap over the coil's connections after every half turn
options.rationale: Describes the split-ring commutator of a dynamo; the two ring systems are readily confused.

options.text: To stop the induced current from reversing inside the coil
options.rationale: Assumes something must prevent the reversal inside the coil, rather than accepting that the coil's pd always alternates.

options.text: To supply the coil with the current it needs to get started
options.rationale: Reads the rings as a power connection into the generator, as a cell would be.

mcqs.stem: A dynamo and an alternator are built identically except for one component. Explain why the dynamo's output potential difference never reverses.

options.text: The induced pd in its coil never reverses direction at all
options.rationale: Reasons backwards from the dc output to a dc source, missing what the commutator does.

options.text: A split-ring commutator swaps the connections each half turn
options.rationale: The induced pd in the coil still reverses, but the connections reverse at the same instant, so the output stays one way round.

options.text: Its coil is spun in the opposite sense to the alternator's
options.rationale: Places the difference in the direction of rotation, the most visible feature of the machine.

options.text: Its magnets are arranged with two north poles facing inwards
options.rationale: Attributes the difference to the magnet arrangement rather than to the connections at the axle.

mcqs.stem: An oscilloscope is connected to an alternator whose coil is being turned steadily. What does the trace of potential difference against time look like?

options.text: A flat horizontal line at a steady positive value
options.rationale: The graph a student draws for any generator if they picture the output as being like a cell's.

options.text: A series of humps that all stay on the positive side
options.rationale: This is the dynamo's trace, chosen by students who have not separated the two machines.

options.text: A wave that rises and falls, going above and below zero
options.rationale: The slip rings pass the coil's reversing potential difference straight to the output, so the trace alternates either side of the zero line.

options.text: A line that rises steadily the longer the coil is spun
options.rationale: Imagines the output building up over time, as though charge were accumulating.

mcqs.stem: Which description matches the potential difference–time graph produced by a dynamo whose coil is turned steadily?

options.text: A horizontal straight line held at one steady value
options.rationale: Equates dc with constant, which is how a cell's output has always been drawn.

options.text: A wave crossing the zero line once every half turn
options.rationale: Gives the alternator's trace, confusing the outputs of the two machines.

options.text: Humps that get taller with every turn of the coil
options.rationale: Suggests the output grows as the machine keeps running, rather than repeating identically.

options.text: Repeated humps, always on the same side of the zero line
options.rationale: The output rises and falls as the coil turns but never reverses, because the commutator swaps the connections each half turn.

mcqs.stem: The coil of an alternator is spun at twice its original steady speed. How does the trace on the oscilloscope change?

options.text: Taller peaks, and the peaks come twice as often
options.rationale: Faster movement induces a larger potential difference, and one rotation gives one cycle, so twice the speed gives twice as many cycles per second.

options.text: The same height peaks, but coming twice as often
options.rationale: Gets the frequency right but keeps the peak height fixed, forgetting that speed affects the size of the induced pd.

options.text: Taller peaks, but coming half as often as before
options.rationale: Gets the height right but stretches the wave out, having lost the link between one rotation and one cycle.

options.text: The same height peaks, coming half as often as before
options.rationale: Wrong on both counts, from a student who reads 'faster' as 'more spread out' and keeps the size fixed.

mcqs.stem: What conversion does a microphone carry out?

options.text: Variations in current into pressure variations in the air
options.rationale: Describes a loudspeaker; the two devices are built alike and are constantly swapped.

options.text: Pressure variations in a sound wave into variations in current
options.rationale: This is the specification's own statement of what microphones do, using the generator effect.

options.text: Pressure variations in a sound wave into a steady direct current
options.rationale: Keeps the input right but assumes the electrical output must be steady, like a supply.

options.text: The loudness of a sound into the frequency of a current
options.rationale: Maps amplitude onto frequency, the standard confusion between the two wave properties.

mcqs.stem: In a moving-coil microphone, what causes the coil to move?

options.text: A current from the amplifier flowing through the coil
options.rationale: Applies the motor effect, as in a loudspeaker, instead of the generator effect.

options.text: The magnet vibrating as the sound wave passes over it
options.rationale: Gets relative movement right but moves the wrong part; the permanent magnet is fixed.

options.text: A diaphragm vibrating as the sound's pressure varies
options.rationale: The pressure variations in the sound wave make the diaphragm vibrate, and the coil is attached to the diaphragm.

options.text: A battery driving the coil to and fro in the magnet's field
options.rationale: Assumes an electrical source must be doing the driving, as in every circuit met before.

mcqs.stem: A singer sings the same note more loudly into a moving-coil microphone. How does the induced current change?

options.text: A current alternating at a higher frequency than before
options.rationale: Maps 'louder' onto frequency instead of amplitude.

options.text: A larger current, but now flowing in one direction only
options.rationale: Gets the size right but assumes a stronger signal must become a one-way current.

options.text: The current is unchanged; only the diaphragm moves more
options.rationale: Breaks the link between the coil's movement and the induced current, as if the coil were driven separately.

options.text: A larger current, alternating at the same frequency
options.rationale: Louder means larger pressure variations, so the diaphragm and coil move further and faster; the pitch, and so the frequency, is unchanged.

mcqs.stem: What does a basic transformer consist of?

options.text: Two coils, a primary and a secondary, wound on an iron core
options.rationale: This is the specification's description of a basic transformer.

options.text: Two coils joined by an iron wire that carries the current
options.rationale: Treats the core as an electrical connection between the two coils.

options.text: One coil wound on an iron core, with a cell in the circuit
options.rationale: Pictures a transformer as a single powered coil rather than two separate circuits.

options.text: Two coils facing each other with an air gap in between
options.rationale: Keeps the two coils but drops the iron core, which is what carries the changing field.

mcqs.stem: Why is the core of a transformer made of iron?

options.text: Because iron conducts electricity well
options.rationale: Follows from believing the core carries current between the coils.

options.text: Because iron is magnetised very easily
options.rationale: The specification gives exactly this reason: iron is used as it is easily magnetised.

options.text: Because iron has a high electrical resistance
options.rationale: Also treats the core electrically, but reasons that it must instead block current.

options.text: Because iron stays magnetised permanently
options.rationale: Confuses an easily magnetised material with a permanent magnet; a core that kept its magnetism could not follow an alternating current.

mcqs.stem: A transformer has 100 turns on its primary coil and 400 turns on its secondary coil. The potential difference across the primary coil is 12 V. What is the potential difference across the secondary coil?

options.text: 3 V
options.rationale: The turns ratio has been applied upside down: 12 × 100/400.

options.text: 4 V
options.rationale: The turns ratio itself, 400/100, handed in as though it were the potential difference.
Vp/Vs = np/ns, so Vs = 12 × 400/100 = 48 V.
The ratio has been added to the primary pd rather than multiplied by it: 12 + 4.

mcqs.stem: A transformer must change a 230 V supply to 11.5 V. The primary coil has 2000 turns. How many turns should the secondary coil have?

options.text: 40 000 turns
options.rationale: The ratio has been inverted: 2000 × 230/11.5, giving more turns for a lower pd.

options.text: 20 turns
options.rationale: The pd ratio 230/11.5 = 20 given as the answer instead of being used to scale the turns.

options.text: 200 turns
options.rationale: The primary turns have been divided by 10 rather than by the pd ratio of 20.

options.text: 100 turns
options.rationale: Vp/Vs = np/ns, so ns = 2000 × 11.5/230 = 100 turns.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes a step-up transformer?

options.text: The secondary pd is greater than the primary pd
options.rationale: The specification states that in a step-up transformer Vs > Vp.

options.text: The secondary pd is smaller than the primary pd
options.rationale: Describes a step-down transformer; students who invert the turns ratio also invert this.

options.text: Both the pd and the current are increased by it
options.rationale: Reads 'step-up' as increasing everything about the supply.

options.text: The power delivered to the circuit is increased
options.rationale: Assumes a transformer can add power rather than trade pd against current.

mcqs.stem: A doorbell needs 6 V and is to be run from the 230 V mains supply. What sort of transformer is needed, and why?

options.text: Step-up, because the secondary has fewer turns than the primary
options.rationale: Recognises that fewer turns are needed but attaches the wrong name, having inverted the relationship.

options.text: Step-down, because the secondary pd is less than the primary
options.rationale: Vs = 6 V is less than Vp = 230 V, which is the definition of a step-down transformer.

options.text: Step-down, because it lowers both the pd and the current
options.rationale: Right name, wrong physics: lowering the pd raises the current for the same power.

options.text: Step-up, because the pd must be raised to drive the bell
options.rationale: Assumes any device needs the pd raised to work, ignoring the values given.

mcqs.stem: What does it mean to say that a transformer is 100% efficient?

options.text: The output pd equals the input pd exactly
options.rationale: Confuses power with potential difference; if the two pds were equal the transformer would do nothing.

options.text: The output current equals the input current
options.rationale: Applies the series-circuit rule that current is the same everywhere.

options.text: The power output equals the power input
options.rationale: The specification states that if transformers were 100% efficient, the electrical power output would equal the electrical power input.

options.text: No current at all flows in the primary coil
options.rationale: Reads 'no waste' as 'nothing used', so the input current is imagined to be zero.

mcqs.stem: A transformer is 100% efficient. The potential difference across its primary coil is 230 V and the current in the primary coil is 0.50 A. The potential difference across the secondary coil is 11.5 V. What is the current in the secondary coil?

options.rationale: The pd ratio has been applied the wrong way round, lowering the current along with the pd.
The current is assumed to be the same in both coils, as it would be in a series circuit.
The pd ratio 230/11.5 = 20 has been given as the current.

mcqs.stem: In the equation Vs × Is = Vp × Ip, what does the quantity Vp × Ip represent?

options.text: The power input to the primary coil
options.rationale: The specification states that Vp × Ip is the power input (primary coil), measured in watts, W.

options.text: The power output from the secondary coil
options.rationale: The subscripts have been swapped; Vs × Is is the power output.

options.text: The current shared by both of the coils
options.rationale: Reads the product as a current, consistent with believing the current is common to both coils.

options.text: The power gained by the transformer core
options.rationale: Treats the transformer as somewhere power is added or stored rather than transferred.

mcqs.stem: Why must a transformer be supplied with an alternating potential difference rather than a steady direct one?

options.text: Direct current cannot pass along the primary coil at all
options.rationale: Assumes the problem is that dc cannot flow, rather than that a steady field induces nothing.

options.text: Only a changing current gives a changing field in the core
options.rationale: An alternating current produces a continuously changing magnetic field in the core, and only a changing field induces a pd across the secondary coil.

options.text: Direct current cannot cross the iron core to the secondary
options.rationale: Still imagines current travelling through the core from one coil to the other.

options.text: Direct current would magnetise the core the wrong way round
options.rationale: Invents a polarity problem instead of identifying the absence of change.

mcqs.stem: A 100% efficient transformer supplies 1.0 kW to a device at 250 V. Its primary coil is connected to a 5000 V supply. What current is drawn from the supply?

options.rationale: This is the secondary current, 1000/250; the student assumes the same current is drawn from the supply.
The secondary current has been scaled by the pd ratio the wrong way round: 4.0 × 5000/250.
The power input equals the power output, so Ip = 1000/5000 = 0.20 A.
The pd ratio 250/5000 has been given as the current, with the power ignored.

mcqs.stem: Why is electrical power transmitted across the National Grid at a very high potential difference?

options.text: A higher pd pushes the current further along the cables
options.rationale: Extends 'voltage pushes current' into a claim about distance travelled.

options.text: The transformers add power, so more arrives at the end
options.rationale: Treats a step-up transformer as a source of extra power.

options.text: A higher pd makes the energy travel along the cables faster
options.rationale: Confuses the size of the potential difference with the speed of energy transfer.

options.text: A smaller current flows, so less energy heats the cables
options.rationale: For a given power, Vs × Is = Vp × Ip means a high pd goes with a small current, and the energy wasted heating the cables depends on the current.

mcqs.stem: A power station transfers 100 MW to the grid. A step-up transformer raises the transmission potential difference from 25 kV to 400 kV. What effect does this have on the transmission cables?

options.text: The current falls, so less energy is wasted heating them
options.rationale: The power transferred is unchanged, so raising the pd by a factor of 16 lowers the current by the same factor, and the heating of the cables falls.

options.text: The current also rises, so more energy is wasted in them
options.rationale: Assumes a step-up transformer raises the current along with the potential difference.

options.text: The current is unchanged, so the heating stays the same
options.rationale: Treats the current as common to both sides of the transformer, as in a series circuit.

options.text: The current falls, so the cables can carry more power
options.rationale: Gets the current right but misstates the benefit; the power transferred is the same, and what improves is the waste.
